name: SSH Brute Force Attack
short_description: Use Hydra to crack weak SSH passwords.
description: Many systems still use weak or default passwords. This lesson teaches you to use Hydra to brute force SSH credentials. The target has username 'root' with a weak password that Hydra will discover.
handler_message:
David Chen. Senior Systems Administrator. TS/SCI clearance. Twenty years at Cerberus.

He started asking questions about NIGHTFALL three weeks ago. Then he disappeared. Police say he left voluntarily. His family filed a missing persons report.

We traced his home IP. His personal workstation is still online at 172.20.0.17. SSH is exposed - unusual for someone with his security background. Unless he wanted someone to find it.

His password habits were... human. Try the obvious first.

Whatever he was gathering, it might still be there.
episode_intro:
David Chen was careful. Twenty years in cybersecurity teaches you paranoia.

But scared people make mistakes. And in his final days at Cerberus, David Chen was very, very scared.

His browser history would tell the story - three weeks of searches for 'NIGHTFALL cerberus,' 'infrastructure attack false flag,' 'whistleblower protection laws.'

He was building a case. Gathering evidence. Trying to figure out who to trust.

Then he vanished.

You're about to walk through his digital footprints. And somewhere, someone is walking through yours.
episode_outro:
David's files confirm your worst fears. Screenshots of internal memos. Deployment schedules. A target list that reads like a map of American infrastructure.

But it's his browser history that chills you. He wasn't just gathering evidence - he was trying to warn someone. Draft emails to journalists, never sent. A half-written post on a whistleblower forum, abandoned.

He found a Tomcat deployment URL buried in the documents. Circled it three times in his notes. Whatever Cerberus is building for NIGHTFALL, it's being staged there.

The deployment server. That's your next target.

But as you disconnect, you notice something in David's recent files: a photograph. Grainy, taken from a distance. A man getting into a black SUV.

The timestamp is from the night David disappeared.

You save the image. Whoever they are, they're not just hiding something. They're willing to make people disappear to keep it hidden.

interstitial.title: Episode 2: WEAK LINKS
interstitial.content:
PREVIOUSLY: You breached Cerberus's forgotten FTP archive. Among the legacy files, one name appeared repeatedly: David Chen.

David was a senior systems administrator with two decades of experience. He had access to everything. And three weeks ago, he started downloading files at an unusual rate.

Then he disappeared.

Police ruled it voluntary departure. His family disagrees. And his home workstation is still online - SSH exposed to the internet.

That's not careless. That's deliberate.

He left a door open. Maybe he wanted someone to find what he found.

steps.title: Verify SSH is running
steps.narrative: SSH on port 22 - the standard secure shell. Version detection will tell us the OpenSSH release, useful for identifying potential vulnerabilities. But today's attack doesn't need a software bug. It needs weak human choices.

steps.title: Create a small wordlist
steps.narrative: Password attacks need wordlists - dictionaries of common passwords. This tiny list covers the basics. Real attacks use rockyou.txt (14 million passwords) or custom lists based on target research. David was scared and distracted. He might have fallen back on something simple.

steps.title: Run Hydra brute force
steps.narrative: Hydra is the industry-standard password cracker. It supports dozens of protocols - SSH, FTP, HTTP, databases, more. The -l flag sets the username, -P provides the password list, -t controls parallel threads. Watch it work through the combinations.

steps.title: Connect via SSH
steps.narrative: Hydra found the password. Now we authenticate legitimately - no exploits, just credentials. This is how most breaches happen. Not sophisticated zero-days, but reused passwords and weak secrets.

steps.title: Accept host key
steps.narrative: First SSH connection to a new host requires accepting its fingerprint. In a real engagement, you'd verify this through another channel to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. For now, accept and proceed.

steps.title: Enter password
steps.narrative: The password Hydra discovered. 'password123' - one of the most common passwords in the world. David Chen knew better. But fear makes people revert to familiar patterns. Whatever he was running from, it was enough to break his operational security.

steps.title: Verify root access
steps.narrative: Confirm your context. You're root on David's workstation. Everything he left behind is accessible. His research. His evidence. Whatever made him a target.

steps.title: One-command pwn
steps.narrative: Once you understand the attack, automation saves time. Exit and run 'pwn ssh' from Kali - it connects directly with the known credentials. Use this for repeated access or demonstrations.

success_criteria: You're logged in as root on David Chen's workstation. His files and research are accessible.
